A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GMsFEM-NO and share the core method and original experiments. All pages, including appendices, equations, figures, tables and v1's checklist, are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original diffusion and Richards-equation experiments, including loss comparisons, solution errors, basis-generation timings and out-of-distribution results in Tables 1–5.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and reports additional results for 3D problems, heat equations, mixed boundary conditions, new comparators and sensitivity studies.

M1.justification: The subspace-learning losses and GMsFEM reconstruction procedure remain unchanged. Section 2.5.1 extends the geometry-specific operator procedure from three domain types in 2D to four in 3D, adding a quarter-domain operator; this is a limited adaptation of the existing method.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only 2D steady diffusion and Richards equations with homogeneous Dirichlet boundaries. v2 adds 3D versions of these problems, a time-dependent 2D heat equation, and diffusion with mixed Dirichlet–Robin boundaries, substantially extending the evaluated problem scope.

E2.justification: v2 adds GNOT and Transolver++ alongside F-FNO in Table 7. Appendix G adds evaluated PCA-Net, kernel, POD, DeepPOD and intrusive methods using DeepONet/F-FNO bases. The four-basis comparison against classical GMsFEM is dropped.

E3.justification: Reported GMsFEM-NO training changes from 800 epochs at 10^-4 to 600 at 10^-3. Standalone F-FNO changes from 10,000-epoch Lion training to 600-epoch AdamW training, with revised architecture and scheduling. Larger-grid, resolution-transfer and sample-size protocols are added, including a 150/50 train/test split for 100^3 problems. These reported changes do not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained loss and forcing-shift experiments, v2 adds training-data sensitivity over 200–800 samples (Table 8), transfer from 100/250 to 500 grid resolution (Table 9), projection-vector-count sensitivity (Table 11), and training-cost amortization analysis (Appendix N). These address new questions about data efficiency, generalization, regularization and practical computational benefit.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run/seed counts, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. v1 explicitly acknowledges this omission in its checklist; v2 removes that checklist but introduces no uncertainty-estimation practice. Its reference to statistical variation is an interpretation, not a statistical analysis.

E6.justification: The original loss scores are retained in v2 Tables 1 and 12, while extensive new benchmark and analysis results are added. Standalone comparisons move to 250×250 with revised training, so differing scores are not same-setting gains. The 100×100 Richards random-to-unit forcing error changes from 2311% to 6503% (v1 Table 5; v2 Table 13). Four-basis classical-GMsFEM and timing results disappear.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix C introduces a projector-distance/Grassmannian derivation for SAL and a proposed solution-error bound, Equation 10, absent from v1. Appendix D adds a formal rotational-invariance argument. These substantially expand the mathematical justification, although the new error bound is not justified as written.

C1.justification: The hybrid solver and subspace-loss contributions remain, but v2 adds central claims of 3D applicability, resolution invariance and greater data efficiency. The introduction narrows v1's better-than-GMsFEM claim to comparable accuracy, while the conclusion extends demonstrated applicability to time-dependent and mixed-boundary problems.

C2.justification: v1 attributes marginal improvements over GMsFEM to more efficient learned subspaces; v2 instead suggests statistical variation. v2 also adds interpretations of data efficiency, size-dependent projection-regularization benefits and costs, inadequate four-basis accuracy, and amortization over repeated simulations. Limitations are updated to acknowledge the new heat and mixed-boundary tests.

D1.justification: v2 adds KLE field-generation instructions and correlation parameters, detailed new-baseline configurations, 3D Fourier-mode choices and training-cost information. Conversely, v1's selected GMsFEM-NO configuration tables and explicit regularization weight of 0.1 are removed; optimal configurations are deferred to a future code release. Neither PDF supplies access to released code.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning beyond neural operators, GMsFEM and Spiridonov et al. It distinguishes learning solution spaces from learned homogenization/upscaling and discusses reduced-order approaches, adding relevant works by Bhattacharya, Kröpfl and others, plus literature supporting the new baselines and Grassmannian analysis.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are substantially rewritten. The loss exposition is reordered, algorithm explanations are revised, and material is reorganized into topical Appendices A–N instead of two training appendices. The NeurIPS checklist is removed.

P2.justification: Figures 2–4 move into appendices, Figure 1's basis-count labels change, and Figure 5 adds accuracy-versus-basis-count curves. Results tables are split, restructured and expanded for new grids, comparators and analyses, while the original configuration tables disappear. The document also adopts a different conference layout.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical scope and limited comparisons through 3D, time-dependent, mixed-boundary, resolution-transfer and broader baseline evaluations. Data-generation disclosure and narrower claims relative to GMsFEM also help. These empirical gains outweigh the lost configuration details and defects in the new supporting analyses: Appendix C's squared-norm bound is unjustified as written, and Table 16's negative break-even counts contradict its cost equation and positive count in the prose. The improvement is principally empirical, not an established theoretical guarantee.
